title: Preseason
author: Chris O’Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien uses the NFL training camp as an analogy for how principals should spend August. The design work of the spring, he argues, exists only on paper, and camp is for installing rather than designing. He asks leaders to give staff a pathway of two or three priorities and a sequenced plan, not just a vision speech, and to pressure-test new systems in live rehearsals while mistakes are cheap. Rehearsals need a calendar slot, leaders who know the levers of each system cold, and feedback given in the moment. He adds that principals must calibrate and coach their leadership team first, because the school will perform at the level of its assistant coaches. The piece ends by noting that preseason also builds the team itself, and warns that schools sink to whatever they practiced in August.
points: O'Brien argues that leaders should replace the opening vision speech with a pathway that names what is being installed, in what order, and what good looks like.
New systems should be rehearsed in August with the adults at full speed, because failing in practice is cheap and failing with students in September is not.
Only the few systems sitting on top of student culture and achievement deserve rehearsal time, so the rehearsal calendar makes priorities concrete.
Calibrating assistant principals, deans and coaches around one standard and giving them reps matters more than any other PD, since the school runs at the ceiling of its leadership team.
quotes: Because here’s the uncomfortable truth about summer design work: right now, your new systems exist only on paper. And no student has ever attended a school on paper.

But your staff doesn’t need you to cast vision nearly as much as they need you to cast a pathway: here are the two or three things we are building this year, here’s why we chose them, here’s what they look like when they’re done well, and here’s exactly how the next three weeks of professional development, practice, and preparation walk us there. A vision tells people where the mountain is. A pathway tells them where to put their feet on Monday.
No coach on earth would do this. The entire point of preseason is that your new schemes fail in August, in practice, where failure is cheap, instead of in September, in the game, where it counts.

You can’t coach a rep you can’t see. Before you rehearse the arrival routine, you have to be able to name — precisely, out loud, without notes — the three or four moves that make it work: where the adults stand, the first words out of their mouths, what happens in the first ten seconds with the kid who comes in hot. Those are the levers. If you can only describe the system in general terms, you’ll watch the rehearsal and see a vibe instead of a mechanism, and your feedback will be “looked pretty good” — which is not feedback.

One AP’s “solid rep” is your “needs to be stopped and rerun,” and if you don’t close that gap in August, your teachers will find it by Labor Day — because the standard in any building quickly becomes whichever leader you happen to get. Calibration is how five leaders become one bar.
A school led by one calibrated leader runs at the ceiling of one person. A school led by five runs at the ceiling of a team — and only one of those survives February.

The season is coming whether you’re ready or not, and here’s the line I keep coming back to, because it’s the whole argument in one sentence: you don’t rise to your mission on a hard Tuesday in February. You sink to whatever you practiced in August.
